EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with continuous treatment intensity, complemented by an event-study for dynamics and a 2SLS robustness check that instruments post-1990 tariffs with the interaction of the industry’s 1983 tariff level and a post-reform dummy.

Rationale  
•  Two dimensions of plausibly exogenous variation exist: (i) time—large, economy-wide liberalisation waves in 1985 and 1990-91, and (ii) cross-industry— industries with high pre-1983 tariffs experience mechanically larger proportional cuts because the new uniform target tariff is exogenous to industry-specific conditions.  
•  A DID that differences wage changes in industries experiencing larger tariff declines from those with smaller declines nets out macro shocks common to all workers.  
•  Parallel-trend credibility can be assessed with pre-period event-study coefficients.  
•  If one worries that contemporaneous tariffs might still be correlated with unobserved industry shocks (e.g., endogenous temporary exemptions), the 2SLS specification offers an additional layer of exogeneity.

================================================================  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment Variable  
TariffCut_jt  ≡  –ΔTariff_jt = (Tariff_j,1983 – Tariff_jt).  
For ease of interpretation we scale it: τ_jt = Tariff_jt / 100 so a one-unit change is a 1 p.p. change in the ad-valorem rate.

Discrete Variant (for graphical DID):  
Treated industries = above-median cumulative tariff cut by 1992;  
Controls = below-median cumulative cut.

Treatment Timing  
Two policy “events”:  
•  Early liberalisation: 1985 (small)  
•  Major liberalisation: 1990-91 (large)  
We code Post_t = 1 for survey years ≥ 1992 (first survey fully after major wave) and 0 otherwise for the baseline binary DID, but the continuous DID uses the exact τ_jt observed in each survey year 1984-1998.

Sample  
Urban wage and salary workers aged 18-60 across all 33 two-digit ISIC industries for which tariff data are available (21 industries) or can be matched by concordance; other sectors serve as additional controls but never receive a tariff measure of zero where coverage is missing.

================================================================  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of tariff reductions, wages in high- and low-pre-tariff industries would have followed the same trend. Plausibility: pre-reform period (1984-1988) shows no systematic difference in wage growth across industries. Highly regulated labour market and capital controls limited pre-trend divergence.  

A2. No Anticipation: Workers and firms did not adjust wages in advance of reforms. Plausibility: reforms were announced only months ahead, negotiated multilaterally, and unexpected at the industry level.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): A tariff cut in industry j does not directly affect wages in industry k beyond general-equilibrium effects we difference out. Reasonable given 2-digit aggregation, but we test for spillovers by excluding closely linked input–output partners.

A4. Composition Stability: Skill distributions within industries are not differentially changing because of the tariff shock. We will control for observables (education, age, gender) and check results in a panel-matched subsample of stayers (those whose industry 2-digit code is the same in t and t-2).  

================================================================  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Industry-specific demand shocks correlated with tariffs (e.g., oil price boom in mining).  
  Mitigation: include industry-year controls (log exports, log imports, world price indices, effective exchange rate), and use the 2SLS strategy with initial tariffs interacted with the post dummy.

T2. Worker Sorting (composition bias).  
  Mitigation: (i) re-estimate on balanced-industry stayers; (ii) run Oaxaca-Blinder-style decompositions of changing observables; (iii) weight industries by pre-period employment to hold constant the employment structure.

T3. Concurrent Policies (1990 labour reform, exchange-rate unification).  
  Mitigation: add interactions of Post_t with industry-level formal-employment share to soak up differential impacts of the labour reform; include year-specific macro controls; event-study will reveal whether breaks coincide with tariff timing rather than 1990 reform date.

================================================================  
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed-effects regressions
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load & merge data -----------------------------------------
workers   <- fread("NHS_workers_1984_1998.csv")    # one row = worker
tariffs   <- fread("tariffs_industry_year.csv")    # industry-level
controls  <- fread("industry_controls.csv")        # exports, imports, etc.

# Industry concordance: assume same 2-digit codes
setkey(workers, industry2, year)
setkey(tariffs,  industry2, year)
w <- merge(workers, tariffs, all.x = TRUE)

setkey(controls, industry2, year)
w <- merge(w, controls, all.x = TRUE)

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------
w[, lnwage := log(annual_earnings / annual_hours)]
w[, tariff_scaled := tariff_percent / 100]                   # e.g., 0.50
w[, pre83_tariff  := tariff_scaled[year == 1983], by = industry2]
w[, post          := as.integer(year >= 1992)]
# Bartik-style instrument
w[, instr_tariff  := pre83_tariff * post]

# Worker controls
w[, educ_dummies := factor(education)]
w[, exper := age - years_schooling - 6]
w[, exper2 := exper^2]

# 3. Main DID specification ------------------------------------
did_mod <- feols(lnwage ~ tariff_scaled | industry2 + year + 
                   educ_dummies + exper + exper2 | 0,  # no IV in this run
                 data = w, weights = ~sample_weight,
                 cluster = ~industry2)

# 4. IV robustness ---------------------------------------------
iv_mod <- feols(lnwage ~ 1 | industry2 + year ~ tariff_scaled | instr_tariff, 
                data = w, weights = ~sample_weight, cluster = ~industry2)

# 5. Event-study graph -----------------------------------------
# Bin leads/lags relative to 1990-91 large cut
w[, rel_year := year - 1991]
# Interaction of rel_year dummies with high-cut indicator
w[, high_cut := (pre83_tariff > median(pre83_tariff, na.rm = TRUE))]
est_mod <- feols(lnwage ~ i(rel_year, high_cut, ref = -1) + 
                 educ_dummies + exper + exper2 | industry2 + year, 
                 data = w, weights = ~sample_weight, cluster = ~industry2)
iplot(est_mod) + labs(title = "Event-study: wage gap, high- vs low-cut industries")

# 6. Robustness: formal workers only ---------------------------
robust_mod <- update(did_mod, data = w[formal == 1])
etable(did_mod, iv_mod, robust_mod, tex = FALSE)
```

================================================================  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory predicts that import-competing sectors lose their mark-up and quasi-rents after protection is removed, compressing the industry-specific component of wages. A 10 percentage-point tariff decrease should reduce wages in that industry by roughly 2–3 percent, after holding worker skill prices fixed. Given average cuts of ~40 p.p. in highly protected sectors, we expect a cumulative wage decline of ~8-12 percent relative to low-cut sectors.

================================================================  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends…….……….. 0.8  
C2: No anticipation…………………………………... 0.7  
C3: No composition changes……………………… 0.6  
C4: No spillovers / interference………………… 0.6  
C5: Exogenous treatment timing/intensity…… 0.8  

(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable). Average ≈ 0.7 – acceptable but warrants the robustness work described above.

================================================================  
This plan leverages plausibly exogenous, differential tariff cuts across industries and time to causally identify how trade liberalisation affected the industry-specific component of Colombian workers’ wages.
